source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

historical_events.event: Docker began as an internal dotCloud project and debuted publicly at PyCon.
Docker 0.9 replaced LXC as default execution environment with libcontainer.
Docker created the Moby project for open research and development.
Docker Desktop licensing changed for larger enterprise users.
Docker acquired AtomicJar.
Docker Engine 28 hardened default container networking.
Docker Desktop 4.41 expanded Docker Model Runner.
Docker Engine 29 made containerd image store default for fresh installations.
VisualDock Server was released according to the source.

semantic_distinctions.name: Image vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Image is a read-only template; container is a runnable managed environment.

semantic_distinctions.name: Container vs Virtual Machine
semantic_distinctions.description: Containers share a host kernel; VMs maintain separate guest environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Namespaces vs cgroups
semantic_distinctions.description: Namespaces isolate views; cgroups limit resources.

semantic_distinctions.name: dockerd vs Docker CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: dockerd is the persistent daemon; CLI is the user-facing command interface.

semantic_distinctions.name: CLI vs Engine API
semantic_distinctions.description: CLI is a client; Engine API is the programmatic request interface served by dockerd.

semantic_distinctions.name: Registry vs Image
semantic_distinctions.description: Registry stores/distributes images; image is the packaged artifact.

semantic_distinctions.name: Compose vs Swarm
semantic_distinctions.description: Compose coordinates multi-container applications; Swarm clusters Docker daemons and services.

semantic_distinctions.name: Service vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Service describes/scales containers across daemons; container is the execution object.

semantic_distinctions.name: Volume vs Container
semantic_distinctions.description: Volume persists independently of container lifecycle.

semantic_distinctions.name: Docker Linux vs Docker macOS
semantic_distinctions.description: Linux can use host kernel directly; macOS uses a Linux VM.

semantic_distinctions.name: Dockerfile vs Image
semantic_distinctions.description: Dockerfile is build instructions; image is resulting read-only template.

semantic_distinctions.name: Push vs Pull
semantic_distinctions.description: Push uploads an image; pull downloads an image.

semantic_distinctions.name: Swarm vs Service
semantic_distinctions.description: Swarm is cluster abstraction; service is scalable workload abstraction inside the swarm.

semantic_distinctions.name: docker context vs docker stack
semantic_distinctions.description: Context targets a Docker host; stack manages Swarm services.

semantic_distinctions.name: Secret vs Volume
semantic_distinctions.description: Source only establishes secret management and volume persistence; they solve different lifecycle/security concerns.

semantic_distinctions.name: Docker Engine vs Docker Desktop
semantic_distinctions.description: Engine is the container engine; Desktop is a desktop product with its own licensing model.

semantic_distinctions.name: Portability vs Isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Packaging enables portability while namespaces/kernel mechanisms provide isolation.

semantic_distinctions.name: libcontainer vs containerd
semantic_distinctions.description: libcontainer is a historical direct-kernel component; containerd becomes the default image store component in Engine 29 per source.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker containers are full virtual machines.
misconceptions.correction: Containers share the host OS kernel; they are OS-level virtualization environments rather than separate guest VMs in the Linux model described.

misconceptions.misconception: A Docker image is the running application.
misconceptions.correction: An image is a read-only template; the container is the runtime object.

misconceptions.misconception: Namespaces and cgroups do the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Namespaces isolate views of resources; cgroups limit CPU/memory resources.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker always runs directly on the host kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source states Docker on macOS uses a Linux virtual machine.

misconceptions.misconception: Dockerfiles are container images.
misconceptions.correction: Dockerfiles are text build specifications that produce images.

misconceptions.misconception: A registry is a running container.
misconceptions.correction: A registry stores/distributes images.

misconceptions.misconception: Compose and Swarm are the same.
misconceptions.correction: Compose manages multi-container applications; Swarm clusters Docker Engines and manages services.

misconceptions.misconception: Deleting a container necessarily deletes persistent data.
misconceptions.correction: Docker Volumes can preserve data independently of container deletion/recreation.

misconceptions.misconception: Swarm updates require one node's approval.
misconceptions.correction: Source states Raft requires majority agreement.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker's CLI is the daemon.
misconceptions.correction: The CLI is a client; dockerd is the persistent daemon.

misconceptions.misconception: EXPOSE alone publishes a port to the network.
misconceptions.correction: Source only states EXPOSE declares a port; it does not state that declaration alone publishes it.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker's Linux runtime has no kernel-level isolation.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly identifies namespaces and cgroups as Linux kernel mechanisms used by Docker.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.
why_it_matters.central_model: Application + dependencies -> Dockerfile/build -> read-only image -> registry distribution -> container runtime -> isolated processes + shared kernel -> Compose/Swarm coordination -> persistent volumes where required.

value: Kubernetes primarily represents desired state as objects; controllers determine corrective actions rather than requiring users to script every individual machine operation.
Control plane coordinates state; nodes execute workloads.
spec expresses desired state; status records current state.
Container is the runtime unit; Pod is the Kubernetes deployable unit that groups one or more containers.
Service provides stable identity/load balancing over a changing set of Pods.
ReplicaSet maintains replica count; Deployment manages ReplicaSets and rollout/rollback.
Stateful workloads require stable identity/order/persistence; stateless workloads generally scale by adding equivalent replicas.
Container filesystems can disappear on restart; volumes provide persistent/shared storage.
CRD defines an API type; Operator combines custom resources with controllers to automate domain-specific behavior.
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may do.
kubelet manages Pod state; runtime executes container lifecycle through CRI.
Pod IPs are tied to individual Pods; Service identity remains stable while matching Pods change.
Namespaces organize/partition resources; authorization determines permitted API actions.
CSI separates storage integration implementation from Kubernetes core.
Scheduler decides where an unscheduled Pod runs; controllers continuously reconcile resource state.
Desired state is declared intent; actual state is observed runtime condition.
Scaling changes capacity/replicas; resilience restores service after failures or drift.
Both externalize configuration, but Secret is intended for confidential data.

value.correction: Kubernetes orchestrates workloads; it can run on virtual machines or bare metal but is not itself the VM hypervisor.

value.misconception: A Pod is just a container
value.correction: A Pod is the deployable unit and can contain one or more co-located containers.

value.misconception: A Service is a Pod with a stable IP
value.correction: A Service is an abstraction over a selected set of Pods and provides stable network identity.

value.misconception: Scheduler keeps desired replica counts
value.correction: Scheduler places unscheduled Pods; controllers reconcile resource state and replica counts.

value.misconception: etcd runs containers
value.correction: etcd stores cluster state; container runtime executes containers on nodes.

value.misconception: Secrets are automatically encrypted at rest
value.correction: The source explicitly notes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default and require additional setup.

value.misconception: Namespace alone provides full security isolation
value.correction: Namespaces partition resources, while authorization controls API permissions.

value.misconception: StatefulSet itself is a database
value.correction: StatefulSet provides identity/order orchestration properties; the database remains the application.

value.misconception: kubelet decides cluster-wide placement

value.misconception: Reconciliation is a one-time deployment step

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized workloads.

source_claims.title: Cluster model
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes assembles virtual or bare-metal computers into a cluster capable of running container workloads.

source_claims.title: Control-plane/node architecture
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes separates management/control-plane components from worker nodes and exposes resources through an object/API model.

source_claims.title: etcd state store
source_claims.claim: etcd persistently represents cluster configuration/state and favors consistency during network partitions.

source_claims.title: API server
source_claims.claim: The API server exposes the Kubernetes API, validates REST requests, persists API-object state, and participates in watch-driven coordination.

source_claims.title: Scheduler
source_claims.claim: The scheduler matches unscheduled Pods to nodes using resource availability and constraints.

source_claims.title: Controllers
source_claims.claim: Controllers reconcile actual cluster state toward desired state and can replace failed workloads.

source_claims.title: kubelet
source_claims.claim: kubelet maintains Pod/container state on each node and reports node status.

source_claims.title: Runtime_CRi
source_claims.claim: The container runtime manages container lifecycle while CRI decouples kubelet from implementation.

source_claims.title: Networking
source_claims.claim: kube-proxy implements network proxy/load-balancing behavior for Services.

source_claims.title: Namespaces
source_claims.claim: Namespaces segregate Kubernetes resources across teams/projects/environments.

source_claims.title: Pods
source_claims.claim: Pods are the basic deployable unit and group one or more co-located containers with a Pod network identity.

source_claims.title: Workloads
source_claims.claim: Higher-level workload objects declaratively manage Pods, including ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

source_claims.title: Services
source_claims.claim: Services provide stable IP/DNS identity and load-balance traffic to Pods selected by labels.

source_claims.title: Storage
source_claims.claim: Volumes, persistent storage, Container Attached Storage, and CSI address storage persistence and external storage integration.

source_claims.title: Configuration
source_claims.claim: ConfigMaps and Secrets externalize configuration; Secrets are intended for confidential data and require additional protection for at-rest encryption.

source_claims.title: API objects
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes objects record intent with metadata, spec, status, ownership, and lifecycle semantics.

source_claims.title: Extensions
source_claims.claim: CRDs, custom controllers, and Operators extend Kubernetes declaratively.

source_claims.title: API security
source_claims.claim: TLS, authentication, and authorization mechanisms protect the Kubernetes API.

source_claims.title: Cluster API
source_claims.claim: Cluster API applies Kubernetes object/API principles to infrastructure and machines.

source_claims.title: Uses
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is used across deployment, scaling, cloud/data-center management, observability, and related infrastructure workflows.

source_claims.title: Complexity/criticism
source_claims.claim: The source discusses complexity, ecosystem fragmentation, operational difficulty, and reasons managed services/PaaS approaches emerged.

source_claims.title: History
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes originated at Google, drew on Borg and Promise Theory, was announced in 2014, and was contributed to CNCF.

source_claims.title: Release timeline
source_claims.claim: The source contains a release/support timeline through Kubernetes 1.36 and related support windows.

central_system_flows: Physical hardware -> hypervisor -> isolated system VM -> guest OS
Host OS -> process VM -> program -> platform-independent execution
Kernel -> OS-level virtualization -> isolated guest environments sharing kernel
Docker -> OS-level virtualization
Snapshot -> overlay layers -> restore
VM state -> migration -> target host/hypervisor

Outer hypervisor -> nested VM -> nested hypervisor

value.name: System VM abstraction
value.expression: Physical hardware -> Hypervisor -> isolated Guest VM -> Guest OS
value.meaning: System virtualization substitutes for a real machine and permits an entire OS to execute in an isolated environment.

value.name: Process VM abstraction
value.expression: Host OS -> Process VM -> Program
value.meaning: A process VM runs as a normal host application and abstracts the underlying hardware/OS for one process.

value.name: OS-level virtualization model
value.expression: Shared kernel + isolated resource views + resource limits -> isolated OS environments
value.meaning: OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel while guest environments share the host OS kernel.

value.name: Snapshot restore model
value.expression: VM state(t_snapshot) + overlays_after_snapshot -> discard overlays -> restored state
value.meaning: Restoring a snapshot disregards changes made after the snapshot point and redirects new changes to a new overlay.

value.name: Migration model
value.expression: VM snapshot/state + target hypervisor -> resumed VM on target host
value.meaning: A VM can be stopped/snapshotted/moved/resumed on another host; synchronized snapshots can reduce interruption.

value.name: Failover model
value.expression: Host failure + last coherent backup state -> VM continuation
value.meaning: Failover continues VM operation from the last-known coherent state available to the backup server.

value.name: Nested virtualization model
value.expression: Outer hypervisor -> VM -> nested hypervisor -> nested guest VM
value.meaning: Nested virtualization recursively places hypervisors/VMs inside another virtualization layer.

value.name: Process VM lifecycle
value.expression: Process start -> VM creation; process close -> VM deletion
value.meaning: The process VM exists for the lifetime of its associated process.

value.name: Same-page memory sharing
value.expression: Identical read-only VM pages -> one physical page
value.meaning: KSM can merge identical pages to improve physical-memory efficiency.

value.name: Full virtualization condition
value.expression: Simulated hardware sufficient for unmodified guest OS
value.meaning: Full virtualization permits an unmodified guest OS designed for the same instruction set to run in isolation.

value.event: System and process virtual machines date to the 1960s; system VMs grew from time-sharing.
IBM CP-40 and CP-67 are identified with early/full virtualization.
Hardware-assisted virtualization was introduced on IBM System/370 for VM/370.
Pascal p-code systems popularized process virtual machines.
Smalltalk-80 VM work advanced JIT compilation.
Java HotSpot incorporated successful VM optimization techniques.
Intel and AMD added additional hardware virtualization support.
Intel Haswell-era VMCS shadowing is cited as accelerating nested virtualization.

value.name: System VM vs Process VM
value.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

value.name: Host vs Guest
value.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

value.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
value.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

value.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
value.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

value.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
value.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

value.name: Snapshot vs Backup
value.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

value.name: Migration vs Failover
value.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

value.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
value.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

value.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
value.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

value.name: JIT vs Interpreter

value.core_problem: Provide abstractions that let software execute as though it has a dedicated computer or portable execution environment while sharing physical computing resources.
value.central_model: Physical hardware -> virtualization layer -> isolated system VM/guest OS OR host OS -> process VM -> portable program.

central_system_flows: Physical hardware -> hypervisor -> isolated system VM -> guest OS
Host OS -> process VM -> program -> platform-independent execution
Kernel -> OS-level virtualization -> isolated guest environments sharing kernel
Docker -> OS-level virtualization
Snapshot -> overlay layers -> restore
VM state -> migration -> target host/hypervisor
Host failure -> backup state -> failover
Outer hypervisor -> nested VM -> nested hypervisor
Compiler -> intermediate representation -> process VM -> machine architecture

equations.name: System VM abstraction
equations.expression: Physical hardware -> Hypervisor -> isolated Guest VM -> Guest OS
equations.meaning: System virtualization substitutes for a real machine and permits an entire OS to execute in an isolated environment.

equations.name: Process VM abstraction
equations.expression: Host OS -> Process VM -> Program
equations.meaning: A process VM runs as a normal host application and abstracts the underlying hardware/OS for one process.

equations.name: OS-level virtualization model
equations.expression: Shared kernel + isolated resource views + resource limits -> isolated OS environments
equations.meaning: OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel while guest environments share the host OS kernel.

equations.name: Snapshot restore model
equations.expression: VM state(t_snapshot) + overlays_after_snapshot -> discard overlays -> restored state
equations.meaning: Restoring a snapshot disregards changes made after the snapshot point and redirects new changes to a new overlay.

equations.name: Migration model
equations.expression: VM snapshot/state + target hypervisor -> resumed VM on target host
equations.meaning: A VM can be stopped/snapshotted/moved/resumed on another host; synchronized snapshots can reduce interruption.

equations.name: Failover model
equations.expression: Host failure + last coherent backup state -> VM continuation
equations.meaning: Failover continues VM operation from the last-known coherent state available to the backup server.

equations.name: Nested virtualization model
equations.expression: Outer hypervisor -> VM -> nested hypervisor -> nested guest VM
equations.meaning: Nested virtualization recursively places hypervisors/VMs inside another virtualization layer.

equations.name: Process VM lifecycle
equations.expression: Process start -> VM creation; process close -> VM deletion
equations.meaning: The process VM exists for the lifetime of its associated process.

equations.name: Same-page memory sharing
equations.expression: Identical read-only VM pages -> one physical page
equations.meaning: KSM can merge identical pages to improve physical-memory efficiency.

equations.name: Full virtualization condition
equations.expression: Simulated hardware sufficient for unmodified guest OS
equations.meaning: Full virtualization permits an unmodified guest OS designed for the same instruction set to run in isolation.

source_claims.claim: A VM virtualizes or emulates a computer system; system VMs execute whole OSs while process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
System VM architecture includes host/guest terminology, historical time-sharing motivations, memory sharing, embedded uses, sandboxing and server consolidation.
Process VMs are host applications supporting one process and provide platform-independent programming environments; cluster-oriented variants abstract communication.
VM history spans 1960s time-sharing, IBM systems, compiler intermediate representations, p-code, Smalltalk, JIT, Self, HotSpot and register-based VMs.
Full virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization are distinct techniques with IBM, Intel and AMD historical milestones and many implementation examples.
OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel, shares the host OS kernel and includes Docker and container technologies.
Snapshots capture VM state/storage; overlays form a coherent virtual disk; migration moves VM state; failover uses last-known coherent backup state.
Nested virtualization recursively runs hypervisors/VMs and may rely on hardware support such as VMCS shadowing.
VMs are used for security isolation and compartmentalization architectures can limit malware spread.

historical_events.event: System and process virtual machines date to the 1960s; system VMs grew from time-sharing.
IBM CP-40 and CP-67 are identified with early/full virtualization.
Hardware-assisted virtualization was introduced on IBM System/370 for VM/370.
Pascal p-code systems popularized process virtual machines.
Smalltalk-80 VM work advanced JIT compilation.
Java HotSpot incorporated successful VM optimization techniques.
Intel and AMD added additional hardware virtualization support.
Intel Haswell-era VMCS shadowing is cited as accelerating nested virtualization.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs Process VM
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

semantic_distinctions.name: Host vs Guest
semantic_distinctions.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

semantic_distinctions.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

semantic_distinctions.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

semantic_distinctions.name: Snapshot vs Backup
semantic_distinctions.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Migration vs Failover
semantic_distinctions.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
semantic_distinctions.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.

fields.label: Central model
fields.value: Application + dependencies -> Dockerfile/build -> read-only image -> registry distribution -> container runtime -> isolated processes + shared kernel -> Compose/Swarm coordination -> persistent volumes where required.

fields.label: Central insight
fields.value: Docker is best understood as a connected packaging, runtime, distribution and orchestration ecosystem: images define reusable software artifacts, containers instantiate them, the Linux kernel supplies isolation/resource primitives, registries distribute artifacts, Compose coordinates applications, and Swarm clusters Docker Engines.

record.description: Reduction of manual operational work through declarative resources and reconciliation.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Central insight
fields.value: Kubernetes is best understood as a distributed control system and extensible API platform, not merely as a tool that 'runs containers'.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Central insight
fields.value: Kubernetes is best understood as a distributed control system and extensible API platform, not merely as a tool that 'runs containers'.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Central insight
fields.value: Kubernetes is best understood as a distributed control system and extensible API platform, not merely as a tool that 'runs containers'.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.
